description: Business-style charts and statistical graphics: bar, pie, sector and bubble charts, histograms, box-and-whisker and distribution charts, quantile and probability plots, plus array and matrix visualizations. These functions understand nested data, associations and weighted categories.

tools.name: BarChart
tools.description: Draws a bar chart from a flat list, a list of groups, or an association whose keys become labels. Nested lists produce grouped or stacked bars depending on ChartLayout. Use it for categorical comparisons and part-to-whole breakdowns.
tools.usage:
BarChart[{y1, y2, ...}, opts]
BarChart[{{a1, a2}, {b1, b2}}, ChartLayout -> "Stacked"]

parameters.name: ChartStyle
parameters.description: Color scheme, e.g. "Pastel" or a list of colors.

parameters.name: BarSpacing
parameters.description: Gap between bars and between groups.

tools.example:
BarChart[<|"Q1" -> 12, "Q2" -> 18, "Q3" -> 9, "Q4" -> 22|>,
  ChartStyle -> "Pastel", ChartLabels -> Automatic, LabelingFunction -> Above]
tools.notes: Bars accept Quantity values and Around values with error bars. BarChart3D gives a 3D version.

tools.name: BarChart3D
tools.description: Draws bars in three dimensions from nested data, which is useful for two-way categorical tables. Rows and columns of the input become the two ground axes. Use sparingly, since 3D bars can occlude one another.

tools.name: PieChart
tools.description: Draws a pie chart where sector angles are proportional to the values. Nested lists produce concentric rings, and SectorOrigin can create donut charts. Use it only for a small number of parts of a single whole.
tools.usage:
PieChart[{v1, v2, ...}, opts]
PieChart[assoc, SectorOrigin -> {Automatic, r}]

parameters.name: SectorOrigin
parameters.description: {angle, inner radius}; a nonzero radius makes a donut.

tools.name: SectorChart
tools.description: Draws sectors whose angle encodes one value and whose radius encodes a second, so each item carries two quantities. It is a compact alternative to a grouped bar chart. Use it for share-versus-magnitude comparisons.

tools.name: RectangleChart
tools.description: Draws rectangles whose width and height each encode a value, producing a two-variable categorical chart. Stacked and grouped layouts are supported. Use it when both an extent and a magnitude matter, such as market size versus margin.

tools.name: BubbleChart
tools.description: Plots triples {x, y, size} as circles positioned in the plane with area proportional to the third value. It shows three variables at once and supports grouping by dataset. Use it for scatter data with an extra weight such as population or revenue.
tools.usage:
BubbleChart[{{x, y, z}, ...}, opts]
BubbleChart[{data1, data2}, opts]

parameters.name: BubbleSizes
parameters.description: {min, max} bubble radii in plot units.

parameters.name: BubbleScale
parameters.description: "Area" or "Diameter" scaling of the third value.

tools.name: Histogram
tools.description: Bins numerical data and draws the counts as bars, choosing bin widths automatically by default. Bin specification and the height function (counts, PDF, CDF, survival) are both controllable. It is the first tool to reach for when exploring a sample distribution.

parameters.name: bspec
parameters.description: Bin width, count, {min, max, dx}, or a method such as "Sturges", "FreedmanDiaconis".

tools.notes: Several datasets can be compared by passing a list of lists. SmoothHistogram gives a kernel-density alternative.

tools.name: Histogram3D
tools.description: Bins bivariate data into a 2D grid and draws the counts as 3D bars. It reveals joint structure that two separate histograms would miss. Use DensityHistogram if occlusion in 3D becomes a problem.

tools.name: DensityHistogram
tools.description: Shows a binned bivariate distribution as a 2D shaded grid, with color encoding the count or density in each cell. It is the flat, readable counterpart of Histogram3D. Use it for large scatter datasets where individual points overplot.

tools.name: SmoothHistogram
tools.description: Draws a kernel-density estimate of a univariate sample as a smooth curve, avoiding the arbitrariness of bin edges. Bandwidth and kernel are adjustable, and PDF/CDF forms are supported. Use it to compare several distributions on one axis.
tools.usage:
SmoothHistogram[data, bw, type, opts]
SmoothHistogram[{data1, data2}, opts]

parameters.name: bw
parameters.description: Bandwidth: a number, Automatic, or a rule such as "SheatherJones".

tools.notes: SmoothHistogram3D and SmoothDensityHistogram handle bivariate samples.

tools.name: BoxWhiskerChart
tools.description: Summarizes one or more samples with box-and-whisker plots showing median, quartiles, whiskers and outliers. Several preset styles control how outliers, means and notches are drawn. Use it to compare distributions across groups compactly.

tools.name: DistributionChart
tools.description: Shows the full shape of each sample as a violin, histogram or point-density strip instead of a five-number summary. It reveals multimodality that a box plot would hide. Use it when distribution shape, not just spread, matters.

tools.name: PairedBarChart
tools.description: Draws two bar series back to back around a shared central axis, the classic population-pyramid layout. It makes symmetry and imbalance between two groups obvious. Use it for male/female, before/after or region-A/region-B comparisons.
tools.example:
PairedBarChart[Range[10], Reverse[Range[10]],
  ChartStyle -> {Blue, Red}, ChartLabels -> {Automatic, None}]

tools.name: PairedHistogram
tools.description: Bins two samples and draws their histograms back to back on a common value axis. It is ideal for directly comparing two distributions of the same quantity. Bin and height specifications match Histogram.

tools.name: PairedSmoothHistogram
tools.description: Draws two kernel-density estimates back to back on a shared axis. It gives a smooth comparison of two samples without bin artifacts. Use it as a two-sample violin plot.

tools.name: QuantilePlot
tools.description: Plots the quantiles of one dataset against those of another dataset or a reference distribution. A straight diagonal indicates that the two share a distribution up to location and scale. Use it as the standard visual goodness-of-fit check.
tools.usage:
QuantilePlot[data]
QuantilePlot[data, dist]
QuantilePlot[data1, data2, opts]
tools.example:
data = RandomVariate[StudentTDistribution[3], 500];
QuantilePlot[data, NormalDistribution[], PlotLabel -> "t(3) vs normal"]
tools.notes: ProbabilityPlot compares CDF values instead of quantiles; DistributionFitTest gives a numeric p-value.

tools.name: ProbabilityPlot
tools.description: Plots the empirical CDF values of data against the CDF of a reference distribution, so a good fit lies on the diagonal. It is bounded in [0,1], which makes tail behaviour easier to read than in a quantile plot. Use it for distribution identification.

tools.name: ProbabilityScalePlot
tools.description: Plots data on axes warped so that a chosen distribution becomes a straight line, the classic probability-paper technique. Supported scales include normal, lognormal, Weibull and exponential. Use it for reliability analysis and quick parameter estimation from the fitted line.

tools.name: ArrayPlot
tools.description: Renders a matrix as a grid of colored cells, one cell per element, with no interpolation. It is extremely fast and exact, which makes it ideal for cellular automata, sparse patterns and label arrays. Specific values can be mapped to explicit colors.

parameters.name: ColorRules
parameters.description: Rules mapping particular values to colors.

tools.example:
ArrayPlot[CellularAutomaton[30, {{1}, 0}, 100],
  ColorRules -> {0 -> White, 1 -> Black}, Frame -> False]

tools.name: MatrixPlot
tools.description: Visualizes the structure of a matrix, emphasizing sparsity pattern, block structure and magnitude. It labels rows and columns with indices and handles SparseArray efficiently. Use it to inspect large linear systems and adjacency matrices.
tools.example:
MatrixPlot[SparseArray[{{i_, i_} -> 2, {i_, j_} /; Abs[i - j] == 1 -> -1}, {80, 80}],
  ColorFunction -> "TemperatureMap"]
tools.notes: ArrayPlot is better when exact per-cell colors matter; MatrixPlot downsamples very large matrices for speed.

tools.name: ReliefPlot
tools.description: Renders an array of heights as a shaded relief image, as if lit from a given direction. Terrain-like structure becomes far easier to see than in a plain density plot. Use it for elevation data, surface metrology and any height field.

parameters.name: LightingAngle
parameters.description: Azimuth (and elevation) of the simulated light source.

tools.example:
ReliefPlot[Table[Sin[x/5] Cos[y/7] + 0.3 RandomReal[], {x, 100}, {y, 100}],
  ColorFunction -> "GreenBrownTerrain", LightingAngle -> Pi/4]

tools.name: WordCloud
tools.description: Lays out words with sizes proportional to their weights or frequencies, packing them into a shape. It accepts raw text, a word list, or an association of word to weight. Use it for a quick qualitative view of text content.
tools.usage:
WordCloud[text]
WordCloud[{w1 -> n1, w2 -> n2, ...}, opts]

parameters.name: MaxItems
parameters.description: Maximum number of words to display.

parameters.name: ColorFunction
parameters.description: Color words by rank or weight.

tools.notes: Give a Region or an Image as a second argument to shape the cloud.

tools.name: TimelinePlot
tools.description: Plots dated events and intervals along a horizontal time axis, stacking them to avoid overlap. It accepts DateObject values, date intervals and entities with dates. Use it for project schedules, historical events and experiment logs.

tools.name: ChartLayout
tools.description: Option for chart functions that selects how multiple data series are arranged, such as grouped, stacked, percentile or step layouts. Changing it is usually the fastest way to switch between absolute and relative comparisons. Valid settings depend on the chart function.

tools.name: ChartElementFunction
tools.description: Option that replaces the default drawing of each chart element with a named preset or a custom function of the element region and value. Presets include gradient bars, glass bars and density shapes. Use it to restyle charts beyond color changes.
tools.notes: ChartElementDataFunction["BarChart"] lists the presets available for a given chart type.

tools.name: ChartStyle
tools.description: Option controlling the colors and directives applied to chart elements, accepting a single directive, a list, a named color scheme or nested specifications for grouped data. It is the primary styling hook for all chart functions. Nested lists style groups and members separately.

tools.name: ChartLabels
tools.description: Option that assigns labels to chart categories, groups and individual elements. Labels can be wrapped in Placed to control their position, such as above the bar or as a radial callout. Use it together with LabelingFunction for value annotations.

tools.name: Callout
tools.description: Labels a curve or point with a leader line pointing to it, choosing a non-overlapping position automatically. It works inside plots, charts and graphics. Use it to annotate specific features without cluttering the legend.
tools.usage:
Callout[expr, label]
Callout[expr, label, pos, opts]
